titleStmt.author: Zoë Slote Morris

bibl.title: The answer is 17 years, what is the question: understanding time lags in translational research
bibl.publisher: Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: A NUMBER IN UNIVERSAL CIRCULATION, WORKED BACKWARDS TO THE DEFINITIONS UNDERNEATH IT - `17 years` for research to reach clinical practice, reviewed across 23 studies that measure different starts, different ends and different things
span.quote: This study aimed to review the literature describing and quantifying time lags in the health research translation process. Papers were included in the review if they quantified time lags in the development of health interventions. The study identified 23 papers. Few were comparable as different studies use different measures, of different things, at different time points. We concluded that the current state of knowledge of time lags is of limited use to those responsible for R&D and knowledge transfer who face difficulties in knowing what they should or can do to reduce time lags. This effectively ‘blindfolds’ investment decisions and risks wasting effort. The study concludes that understanding lags first requires agreeing models, definitions and measures, which can be applied in practice.

span.label: what was actually measured to produce the time lags that health research policy is built on, and whether the figures can be compared or added at all
span.quote: As is shown in Table 1 , studies of time lags in translation of research to practice often measure different points in the process. For example, Decullier et al. 28 and Stern and Simes 29 measure time between ethical approval and date of first publication; Grant et al. 30 and HERG et al. 13 look at publication to guideline; DiMasi calculated the length of time within and between phases in US drug development to calculate the costs associated with the phases. Sternitzke looked at commercialization of pharmaceutical innovations from ‘chemical synthesis’ to FDA approval. 32 Ioannidis attempted to estimate the time lag between date of trial registration and several milestones to publication. Grant et al. , Mansfield and Comroe and Dripps work backwards from practice to publication.

span.label: a conceptual model of the translation pipeline with every reviewed study's start point and end point mapped onto it, and the finding that the studies are not measuring the same quantity
span.quote: Limitations of the literature examined include the use of proxy measures. Much of the literature on lags focuses on dissemination and publication in peer-review journals in particular as these are the most measureable. If there are significant lags in, say, the grant or ethics process, this is less likely to be reflected in current total lag estimations. Moreover, the variation in choice of proxy measures means that studies are almost never measuring the same thing, making valid aggregation and generalization difficult.

span.label: critique
span.quote: There is a clear trend in the literature to seek a single answer to a single question through the calculation of an average. The variation found in the literature suggests that this is not possible (or even desirable), and variation matters. Moreover, many of the published ‘averages’ are derived from adding an empirically derived mean duration for one section of journey from one point in time, in one topic, and adding it to other parts without reflection.

span.label: a literature that converges on one figure for a quantity it has never defined, and a policy apparatus that spends against that figure
span.quote: It is frequently stated that it takes an average of 17 years for research evidence to reach clinical practice. 1 , 3 , 15 Balas and Bohen, 16 Grant 17 and Wratschko 18 all estimated a time lag of 17 years measuring different points of the process. Such convergence around an ‘average’ time lag of 17 years hides complexities that are relevant to policy and practice

span.label: a non-exhaustive multi-strategy review - formal search, backward and forward citation tracking, targeted journals - with a data-extraction template recording each study's start date, end date, range, mean, median, topic and country
span.term: a non-exhaustive multi-strategy review - formal search, backward and forward citation tracking, targeted journals - with a data-extraction template recording each study's start date, end date, range, mean, median, topic and country
span.quote: This study aimed to review the literature describing and quantifying time lags in the health research translation process. Papers were included in the review if they quantified time lags in the development of health interventions. The study identified 23 papers. Few were comparable as different studies use different measures, of different things, at different time points. We concluded that the current state of knowledge of time lags is of limited use to those responsible for R&D and knowledge transfer who face difficulties in knowing what they should or can do to reduce time lags. This effectively ‘blindfolds’ investment decisions and risks wasting effort. The study concludes that understanding lags first requires agreeing models, definitions and measures, which can be applied in practice.

span.label: **THREE STUDIES AGREE ON 17 YEARS, AND THE EXPLANATION OFFERED IS ABOUT THE INSTRUMENT RATHER THAN THE WORLD**: `Using DIFFERENT ENDPOINTS, DIFFERENT DOMAINS AND DIFFERENT APPROACHES, Balas and Bohen and Grant et al. BOTH ESTIMATE THE TIME LAG ... BEING 17 YEARS ... IT IS SURPRISING THAT 17 IS THE ANSWER TO SEVERAL RELATED BUT DIFFERING QUESTIONS. IS THIS COINCIDENCE OR NOT? ONE POSSIBLE REASON FOR THE CONVERGENCE IS THE DIFFICULTY OF MEASURING LONGER LAGS ... WHICH PROVIDES A CEILING TO SUCH ESTIMATES.` **Agreement between measurements is read as a property of the ruler**, which is the strongest form of `an instrument's first output is itself`
span.quote: Using different endpoints, different domains and different approaches, Balas and Bohen 16 and Grant et al. 30 both estimate the time lag in health research being 17 years. Wratschko also suggested 17 years as the highest limit for the time taken from drug discovery to commercialization. It is surprising that 17 is the answer to several related but differing questions. Is this coincidence or not? One possible reason for the convergence is the difficulty of measuring longer lags – because of limitations of citation indexes, other records and recollections – which provides a ceiling to such estimates and leads to a convergence of average lags.

span.label: **AND THE CANONICAL 17 IS WRONG BY SIX YEARS ONCE ITS ASSEMBLY IS ACCOUNTED FOR**: `Balas and Bohen calculate an average of 17 years from original research to practice formed from ADDING TOGETHER A NUMBER OF SINGLE STUDIES OF DIFFERENT PHASES including one that estimates a lag of 6-13 years. ACCOUNTING FOR THIS CHANGES THEIR ESTIMATE of the time lag between journal submission to use in practice FROM BETWEEN 17 YEARS TO 23 YEARS.` The most-quoted figure in translational research, restated as 23
span.quote: Some studies aggregate data from earlier studies without critical reflection or recognition of this. 16 , 25 For example, Balas and Bohen calculate an average of 17 years from original research to practice formed from adding together a number of single studies of different phases including one that estimates a lag of 6–13 years. Accounting for this changes their estimate of the time lag between journal submission to use in practice from between 17 years to 23 years.

span.label: **AND THE NUMBER SETS A NATIONAL RATE OF RETURN**: `This level of benefit was calculated using AN ESTIMATED LAG OF 17 YEARS. VARYING THE LAG TIME FROM 10 TO 25 YEARS PRODUCED RATES OF RETURN OF 13% AND 6%, RESPECTIVELY.` An internal rate of return on thirty years of UK cardiovascular research moves by a factor of two on the choice of a definition nobody in the literature shares. **This is the clearest case in the corpus of a definitional choice with a monetary consequence**
span.quote: This level of benefit was calculated using an estimated lag of 17 years. Varying the lag time from 10 to 25 years produced rates of return of 13% and 6%, respectively, illustrating that shortening the lag between bench and bedside improves the overall benefit of cardiovascular research.

span.label: AND THE STUDIES ARE NOT MEASURING ONE QUANTITY: `Much of the literature on lags focuses on dissemination and publication in peer-review journals in particular AS THESE ARE THE MOST MEASUREABLE ... the variation in choice of proxy measures means that STUDIES ARE ALMOST NEVER MEASURING THE SAME THING, MAKING VALID AGGREGATION AND GENERALIZATION DIFFICULT.` **The proxy was chosen for being measurable, not for being the thing** - and the consequence is that the figures cannot be added
span.quote: Limitations of the literature examined include the use of proxy measures. Much of the literature on lags focuses on dissemination and publication in peer-review journals in particular as these are the most measureable. If there are significant lags in, say, the grant or ethics process, this is less likely to be reflected in current total lag estimations. Moreover, the variation in choice of proxy measures means that studies are almost never measuring the same thing, making valid aggregation and generalization difficult.

span.label: **AND A STATISTIC THAT CHANGED ITS NAME IN TRANSIT**: `Decullier et al. report `MEAN` LAGS, and Dwan, IN REPORTING DECULLIER ET AL., IN THEIR REVIEW REFER TO `MEDIAN` LAGS. NEITHER REPORTS DISTRIBUTIONS. Ranges - or even INTERQUARTILE RANGES AS LARGE AS 221 YEARS - are seldom reported.` A mean becomes a median between a paper and its reviewer, and neither publishes the distribution that would settle it
span.quote: Measurement and reporting is often poor. For example, Decullier et al. report ‘mean’ lags, 28 and Dwan, in reporting Decullier et al. , in their review refer to ‘median’ lags. Neither reports distributions. Ranges – or even interquartile ranges as large as 221 years 38 – are seldom reported.

span.label: AND AN AVERAGE THAT HIDES A RANGE LARGER THAN ITSELF: `clinical trials with null or negative results `ON AVERAGE` took `JUST OVER A YEAR LONGER` to be published than those with positive results. This average is associated with A RANGE OF SIX TO EIGHT YEARS for studies with a negative or null result, COMPARED WITH FOUR TO FIVE YEARS for those with positive results. Comparing the slowest negative publication with the fastest positive publication MAKES A POTENTIAL DIFFERENCE OF FOUR YEARS - HALF OF THE MAXIMUM LAG.` The headline is one year; the spread is four
span.quote: For example, Hopewell et al. in their review of publication bias conclude that clinical trials with null or negative results ‘on average’ took ‘just over a year longer to be published than those with positive results’. This average is associated with a range of six to eight years for studies with a negative or null result, compared with four to five years for those with positive results. Comparing the slowest negative publication with the fastest positive publication makes a potential difference of four years – half of the maximum lag.

span.label: AND THE FIELD'S HABIT IS NAMED: `THERE IS A CLEAR TREND IN THE LITERATURE TO SEEK A SINGLE ANSWER TO A SINGLE QUESTION THROUGH THE CALCULATION OF AN AVERAGE. The variation found in the literature suggests that THIS IS NOT POSSIBLE (OR EVEN DESIRABLE), AND VARIATION MATTERS. Moreover, many of the published `averages` are derived from ADDING an empirically derived mean duration for one section of journey from one point in time, in one topic, AND ADDING IT TO OTHER PARTS WITHOUT REFLECTION.` **A summary statistic assembled from incommensurable parts**
span.quote: There is a clear trend in the literature to seek a single answer to a single question through the calculation of an average. The variation found in the literature suggests that this is not possible (or even desirable), and variation matters. Moreover, many of the published ‘averages’ are derived from adding an empirically derived mean duration for one section of journey from one point in time, in one topic, and adding it to other parts without reflection.

span.label: AND THE TERM ITSELF MEANS DIFFERENT THINGS TO DIFFERENT PEOPLE, ON THE RECORD: `Woolf has argued that `TRANSLATION RESEARCH MEANS DIFFERENT THINGS TO DIFFERENT PEOPLE` and this is reflected in the various models and definitions found in the literature. However, as translational research also `SEEMS IMPORTANT TO ALMOST EVERYONE` there would seem to be benefit in trying to unify models and definitions.` The two halves of the problem in one sentence: **maximum importance, minimum agreement**
span.quote: Woolf has argued that ‘translation research means different things to different people’ 23 and this is reflected in the various models and definitions found in the literature. However, as translational research also ‘seems important to almost everyone’ 23 there would seem to be benefit in trying to unify models and definitions.

span.label: AND ONE OF THE TWO PHASE NAMES IS FLAGGED BY ITS OWN USERS AS CONFUSING: `Type 1 translation, ALSO SOMEWHAT CONFUSINGLY CALLED `BENCH TO BEDSIDE`, refers to the conversion of knowledge from basic science research into a potential clinical product FOR TESTING ON HUMAN SUBJECTS` - while Type 2, `research into practice`, is the one that actually reaches the bedside. **The metaphor names the wrong end of the pipeline**
span.quote: ‘Translational research’ is typically separated into two phases of research. Type 1 translation, also somewhat confusingly called ‘bench to bedside’, refers to the conversion of knowledge from basic science research into a potential clinical product for testing on human subjects. Type 2 translation, ‘research into practice’, tends to refer to the process of converting promising interventions in clinical research into healthcare practice (thus is closer to the notion of the ‘bedside’).

span.label: AND THE GAPS THE POLICY TARGETS ARE THE LEAST WELL DEFINED PART: `Conceptual models typically include `TRANSLATIONAL GAPS`, which describe the movement from one phase of research to another. Each of these is also associated with delays, ALTHOUGH PRECISELY WHAT AND WHERE THESE GAPS ARE, AND HOW LONG THEY ARE, IS AGAIN NOT CONSISTENT IN THE LITERATURE. POLICY MEASURES TO EXPEDITE THE TRANSLATION PROCESS TYPICALLY FOCUS ON THESE GAPS.` Intervention is aimed at the part with no agreed boundaries
span.quote: Conceptual models typically include ‘translational gaps’, which describe the movement from one phase of research to another. Each of these is also associated with delays, although precisely what and where these gaps are, and how long they are, is again not consistent in the literature.

span.label: AND THE VARIATION SURVIVES INSIDE A SINGLE TOPIC: `examining research relating to advances in neonatal care, Grant et al. traced research papers back through four `GENERATIONS` of publication. They found `the overall time between generations 1 to 4 RANGES FROM 13 YEARS (for artificial surfactant) TO 21 YEARS (for parenteral nutrition). The other three advances TOOK 17 YEARS to develop through four generations of citations`.` One method, one clinical area, five interventions, and an eight-year spread
span.quote: For example, examining research relating to advances in neonatal care, Grant et al. traced research papers back through four ‘generations’ of publication. They found ‘the overall time between generations 1 to 4 ranges from 13 years (for artificial surfactant) to 21 years (for parenteral nutrition). The other three advances took 17 years to develop through four generations of citations’.

span.label: AND THE LAG RUNS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: `it took SIX YEARS for a review of evidence supporting the use of thrombolytic drugs to result in a standard recommendation, WHEREAS PROPHYLACTIC LIDOCAINE WAS USED WIDELY IN PRACTICE FOR 25 YEARS BASED ON NO EVIDENCE OF EFFECTIVENESS.` A field whose central complaint is that evidence reaches practice too slowly, with a case of practice arriving twenty-five years AHEAD of any evidence at all
span.quote: study of treatment for myocardial infarction yielded similar results: it took six years for a review of evidence supporting the use of thrombolytic drugs to result in a standard recommendation, whereas prophylactic lidocaine was used widely in practice for 25 years based on no evidence of effectiveness.

span.label: ONLY ONE STUDY MEASURES THE THING EVERYONE QUOTES THE NUMBER FOR: `Table 1 also points to two substantive gaps in knowledge: THE TIME LAG INVOLVED IN AND BETWEEN DISCOVERY AND DEVELOPMENT (T1), and THE TIME LAG BETWEEN PUBLICATION TO PRACTICE. ONLY ONE STUDY HAS `IMPLEMENTATION` INTO PRACTICE AS ITS ENDPOINT.` The `17 years to reach clinical practice` figure rests on a single measurement of reaching clinical practice
span.quote: Table 1 also points to two substantive gaps in knowledge: the time lag involved in and between discovery and development (T1), and the time lag between publication to practice. Only one study has ‘implementation’ into practice as its endpoint.

span.label: AND THE AUTHORS PUT THEIR OWN SEARCH'S WEAKNESS FIRST: `Despite our attempts to be comprehensive, however, WE ARE AWARE THAT STUDIES OF TIME LAGS IN HEALTH RESEARCH ARE WIDELY DISTRIBUTED AND NOT EASILY IDENTIFIED USING FORMAL LITERATURE SEARCHES and we may have failed to capture relevant studies.` The Methods say the same before the results: `Our search WAS NOT INTENDED TO BE EXHAUSTIVE`
span.quote: This study aimed to review the literature describing and quantifying time lags in the health research translation process. Papers were included in the review if they quantified time lags in the development of health interventions. The study identified 23 papers. Few were comparable as different studies use different measures, of different things, at different time points. We concluded that the current state of knowledge of time lags is of limited use to those responsible for R&D and knowledge transfer who face difficulties in knowing what they should or can do to reduce time lags. This effectively ‘blindfolds’ investment decisions and risks wasting effort. The study concludes that understanding lags first requires agreeing models, definitions and measures, which can be applied in practice.

span.label: AND THE MODEL THEY BUILD IS LINEAR AND THEY SAY SO: `Clearly this model CAN BE CRITIQUED FOR BEING LINEAR and we acknowledge the considerable literature that challenges this notion and ACCEPT THAT RESEARCH TRANSLATION IS A MESSY, ITERATIVE AND COMPLEX PROCESS ... At the same time, we would argue that FOR THE PURPOSES OF UNDERSTANDING AND CONCEPTUALISING TIME LAGS THE MODEL IS APPROPRIATE.` A simplification defended by its purpose rather than its accuracy
span.quote: Clearly this model can be critiqued for being linear and we acknowledge the considerable literature that challenges this notion and accept that research translation is a messy, iterative and complex process (see Balaconi et al. for a good review of the liner models critiques and their partial rebuttal 24 ). At the same time, we would argue that for the purposes of understanding and conceptualising time lags the model is appropriate in showing common steps found in the literature.

span.label: AND THE LAGS ARE NOT STABLE OVER TIME, SO A FIGURE ALSO HAS A DATE: `Pulido noted a difference of 0.9 years or 0.3 years from acceptance to publication IN 1992 AND 1982, RESPECTIVELY. DiMasi reported a slight shortening of the approval process between 1991 and 2003. Tsuiji and Tsutani reported REDUCED LAGS in the drug approval process in Japan FOLLOWING A CHANGE IN POLICY to try and expedite it.` A quantity that moves when policy moves, quoted as a constant
span.quote: Studies also show that time lags are not stable over time. For example, Pulido noted a difference of 0.9 years or 0.3 years from acceptance to publication in 1992 and 1982, respectively. DiMasi reported a slight shortening of the approval process between 1991 and 2003. Tsuiji and Tsutani reported reduced lags in the drug approval process in Japan following a change in policy to try and expedite it.

span.label: the 17-year translation lag is a figure produced by an economic calculation of the returns to medical research, including spillovers to the wider economy
span.quote: (The remaining 30% arise from ‘spillovers’ benefiting the wider economy.) This level of benefit was calculated using an estimated lag of 17 years.

span.label: mapping each reviewed study's start point and end point onto one conceptual model before comparing any figures
span.note: eliminates: adding or averaging intervals that do not denote the same quantity · outcome: held
span.quote: Understanding time lags requires a conceptual model of how research in science is converted to patient benefit so that the durations of activities and waits can be measured.

span.note: eliminates: missing a scattered literature that database indexing does not group · outcome: partial

Neither reports distributions. Ranges – or even interquartile ranges as large as 221 years 38 – are seldom reported.

span.quote: Based on the review, and our own work on lags, 13 , 17 , 19 , 30 , 51 we would argue that an essential step to being able to quantify time lags, and thereby make improvements, requires stakeholders to agree definitions, key stages and measures.

span.note: the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.95 — `UNDERSTANDING TIME LAGS REQUIRES A CONCEPTUAL MODEL of how research in science is converted to patient benefit SO THAT THE DURATIONS OF ACTIVITIES AND WAITS CAN BE MEASURED.` The operationalisation is the whole argument: 23 studies each picked two markers off an unstated model, and the figures cannot be added because the models were never the same

span.quote: Limitations of the literature examined include the use of proxy measures. Much of the literature on lags focuses on dissemination and publication in peer-review journals in particular as these are the most measureable. If there are significant lags in, say, the grant or ethics process, this is less likely to be reflected in current total lag estimations. Moreover, the variation in choice of proxy measures means that studies are almost never measuring the same thing, making valid aggregation and generalization difficult.
